questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Define the money supply in a beekeeper's ledger
questions.stem: A beekeeper's ledger lists currency and checkable deposits as the money supply.

options.text: Currency plus checkable deposits equals M1
Currency alone equals M1
options.misconception: omits checkable deposits from narrow money

options.text: Savings accounts alone equal M1
Certificates of deposit equal M1

questions.explanation: M1 includes currency in circulation plus checkable deposits. Savings and time deposits are broader measures, not M1.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain fractional reserve banking in a hive credit union
questions.stem: A hive credit union holds ten percent reserves against honey-backed deposits.

options.text: It lends out the full one hundred percent of deposits
It lends out the remaining ninety percent of deposits
It lends out only the reserve portion
It cannot lend because reserves are required
options.misconception: confuses required reserves with a lending ban

questions.explanation: Under fractional reserves a bank keeps a fraction and lends the rest. With ten percent reserves, ninety percent is lendable.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify an error in a money multiplier claim
questions.stem: A logbook claims the simple money multiplier is the reserve ratio itself rather than its reciprocal.

options.text: The multiplier equals deposits times reserves
The claim is correct as stated
The claim reverses the multiplier and the ratio
The multiplier equals one plus the ratio

questions.explanation: The simple money multiplier is one divided by the reserve ratio, not the ratio. Reversing them understates expansion capacity.
questions.hint: Multiplier is one over the ratio.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain M2 in a beekeeper's account records
questions.stem: Explain what M2 adds to M1 in a beekeeper's bank account records.

answer.exemplar: M2 adds savings deposits, small time deposits, and retail money market funds to M1, capturing near-money assets that are less liquid than checking balances.

questions.explanation: M2 broadens M1 by adding savings, small time deposits, and retail money funds. These are near-money assets.
questions.hint: M2 adds savings and small time deposits.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute deposit expansion from new reserves
questions.stem: With a reserve ratio of twenty percent, how much total deposits result from ten thousand in new reserves?
questions.explanation: The multiplier is five, so ten thousand times five equals fifty thousand in total deposits. Each round keeps twenty percent and lends eighty percent.
questions.hint: Multiply reserves by one over the ratio.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify bank assets on a balance sheet
questions.stem: If a hive bank has loans of forty thousand and reserves of ten thousand, what are total assets?
questions.explanation: Bank assets include loans plus reserves, so forty thousand plus ten thousand equals fifty thousand. Liabilities are deposits.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how banks earn profit
questions.stem: A logbook asks how a hive bank earns profit from deposits.

options.text: It earns profit only from central bank transfers
It keeps all deposits as reserves and charges fees only
It pays depositors more than it charges borrowers
It lends deposits at higher rates than it pays depositors

questions.explanation: Banks profit from the spread between lending rates and deposit rates. Keeping all reserves as cash would not be profitable.
questions.hint: Profit comes from the rate spread.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the money multiplier from a reserve ratio
questions.stem: A central bank bulletin sets the reserve ratio at five percent for hive banks.

options.text: The money multiplier is five
options.misconception: confuses the ratio with the multiplier

options.text: The money multiplier is twenty
The money multiplier is zero point zero five
options.misconception: uses the ratio as the multiplier

options.text: The money multiplier is ninety five

questions.explanation: The simple multiplier is one over zero point zero five, or twenty. A low reserve ratio permits large expansion.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify central bank assets

The claim is correct as stated
The claim omits government securities and reserves
Central banks hold no assets at all

questions.explanation: Central bank assets include government securities and loans to banks, while currency in circulation is a liability. The claim is incomplete.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the real multiplier is smaller
questions.stem: Explain why the real-world money multiplier is smaller than the simple multiplier in a hive economy.

answer.exemplar: The real-world multiplier is smaller because households hold currency and banks hold excess reserves, both of which reduce the funds available for repeated lending.

questions.explanation: Currency drain and excess reserves reduce the actual expansion below the simple multiplier. The simple formula ignores both leakages.
questions.hint: Currency and excess reserves reduce expansion.

questions.learningObjective: Compute new deposits from a loan
questions.stem: If a hive bank lends five thousand with a twenty percent reserve ratio, how much new deposit is created when the loan is spent and redeposited?
questions.explanation: The loan becomes a new deposit of five thousand when spent and redeposited. Reserves are held against it in the next round.
questions.hint: The loan equals the new deposit.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute required reserves from deposits
questions.stem: With deposits of one hundred thousand and a ten percent reserve ratio, what are required reserves?
questions.explanation: Required reserves equal deposits times the ratio, so one hundred thousand times zero point one equals ten thousand. The rest is excess reserves.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a single loan creates deposits
questions.stem: A beekeeper asks how a single bank loan creates new deposits.

options.text: Deposits are created only by the central bank
The loan is kept as cash by the borrower
The bank creates deposits without making a loan
The loan is spent and the proceeds are redeposited

questions.explanation: A loan creates a deposit that is spent and redeposited, expanding the money supply. If cash is hoarded, expansion stops.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bank runs threaten solvency
questions.stem: A logbook shows depositors withdrawing funds faster than reserves can cover.

options.text: The bank is safe because reserves equal deposits
The bank may fail because reserves are fractional
Withdrawals increase bank reserves
options.misconception: reverses the reserve effect of withdrawals

options.text: The central bank must buy bank assets
options.misconception: misstates the lender of last resort role

questions.explanation: Banks hold only fractional reserves, so mass withdrawals can exhaust reserves and cause failure. This is the core bank run risk.

The statement is correct

options.text: The statement confuses M1 with M2
Savings accounts are not money at all
options.misconception: denies the money status of savings

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why banks keep reserves
questions.stem: Explain why a hive bank keeps reserves instead of lending all deposits.

answer.exemplar: A bank keeps reserves to meet depositor withdrawals and satisfy regulatory requirements, while lending the excess to earn profit from interest.

questions.explanation: Reserves cover withdrawals and meet requirements; excess reserves are lent for profit. Lending everything would risk illiquidity.

questions.stem: What is the simple money multiplier when the reserve ratio is twelve point five percent?

questions.explanation: M1 equals currency plus checkable deposits, so thirty thousand plus seventy thousand equals one hundred thousand. Savings are excluded.

options.text: Expansion stops because borrowers hoard cash
The claim is correct because reserves are exhausted
Only the central bank can continue expansion
Expansion continues through repeated lending and redepositing

questions.explanation: Deposit expansion continues through repeated rounds until reserves are fully held. The first round is only the beginning.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the balance sheet identity
questions.stem: Explain why a hive bank's assets must equal its liabilities plus equity.

answer.exemplar: The balance sheet identity requires assets to equal liabilities plus equity, so any change in loans or deposits must be matched by an offsetting change on the other side.

questions.explanation: Assets equal liabilities plus equity by accounting identity. A loan asset is funded by deposits or equity.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute bank profit from interest spread
questions.stem: If a hive bank earns six percent on loans and pays two percent on deposits, what is the spread?
questions.explanation: The spread is six percent minus two percent, or four percentage points. The spread drives bank profitability.
questions.hint: Subtract deposit rate from loan rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute total money creation from reserves
questions.stem: With a reserve ratio of twenty five percent, how much money is created from twenty thousand in new reserves?
questions.explanation: The multiplier is four, so twenty thousand times four equals eighty thousand. New reserves support multiple deposits.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a central bank liability
questions.stem: A logbook lists items on a central bank balance sheet.

options.text: Currency in circulation is an asset
Currency in circulation is a liability
Government securities are liabilities
Bank reserves are equity

questions.explanation: Currency in circulation is a liability of the central bank, while government securities are assets. Bank reserves are also liabilities.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a factor reducing the real multiplier
questions.stem: A hive bank report shows excess reserves rising during a downturn.

options.text: Excess reserves do not affect the multiplier
Excess reserves increase the real multiplier
Excess reserves reduce the real money multiplier
Excess reserves equal required reserves

questions.explanation: Excess reserves reduce the funds lent, lowering the real multiplier below the simple formula. Banks hold them for safety.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the relationship between loans and deposits
questions.stem: Explain why a bank loan and a deposit are two sides of the same transaction.

answer.exemplar: When a bank makes a loan it credits the borrower's deposit account, so the loan asset and the deposit liability are created simultaneously in the same transaction.

questions.explanation: A loan creates a matching deposit liability simultaneously. The two entries are the two sides of one transaction.

The claim is correct
Requirements only affect deposits, not loans
Raising requirements reduces lendable funds

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS

questions.stem: If a bank lends eight thousand with a twenty percent reserve ratio, how much total deposit expansion can follow?
questions.explanation: The loan of eight thousand supports expansion with a multiplier of five, so total deposits can reach forty thousand. Reserves are held at each round.

questions.explanation: The shortfall is withdrawals minus reserves, or twenty thousand. Fractional reserves cannot cover full withdrawals.

options.text: M2 is the narrowest measure
M1 is the narrowest measure
M3 is the narrowest measure
All measures are equally narrow

questions.explanation: M1 is the narrowest money measure, containing the most liquid assets. M2 and M3 add less liquid assets.

options.misconception: misreads reserve requirements as a ban

options.text: Fractional reserves mean all deposits are kept as cash
Fractional reserves allow lending while keeping some cash
Fractional reserves eliminate bank runs

questions.explanation: Fractional reserves let banks lend most deposits while keeping a fraction for withdrawals. Full reserves would forbid lending.

The claim is correct

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between M1 and M2
questions.stem: Explain the difference between M1 and M2 in a beekeeper's accounts.

answer.exemplar: M1 contains the most liquid money like currency and checking balances, while M2 adds savings and small time deposits that are less immediately spendable.

questions.explanation: M1 is the most liquid money; M2 adds savings and small time deposits. The difference is liquidity.

questions.stem: If a hive bank has assets of one hundred thousand and equity of ten thousand, what are its deposits?

questions.learningObjective: Identify an error in a profitability claim

options.text: The claim is correct
Profit mainly comes from the interest spread on loans
Profit comes from reserve requirements
Profit comes from central bank transfers

questions.explanation: The core profit source is the spread between loan and deposit rates. Fees supplement but do not replace lending income.

options.text: The multiplier is unchanged at ten
The money multiplier falls from ten to five
The money multiplier rises from ten to twenty
The multiplier becomes zero

questions.stem: A bulletin shows the central bank buying bonds from hive banks.

Bank reserves and the monetary base fall
Only currency in circulation changes
Bank reserves and the monetary base rise

questions.learningObjective: Compute lendable funds after reserves
questions.stem: With deposits of sixty thousand and a ten percent reserve ratio, how much can a hive bank lend?
questions.explanation: Required reserves are six thousand, so lendable funds are fifty four thousand. Lending that amount creates new deposits.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of reserve requirements
questions.stem: Explain why regulators impose reserve requirements on hive banks.

answer.exemplar: Reserve requirements ensure banks keep enough liquid funds to meet withdrawals and limit excessive money creation, supporting financial stability.

questions.explanation: Reserve requirements provide liquidity for withdrawals and constrain money creation, supporting stability. They also shape the multiplier.

Loans also create deposits when credited to accounts
Deposits are created by the central bank alone
Deposits cannot be created, only moved

questions.explanation: Deposits arise both from cash deposits and from loan proceeds credited to accounts. The cash-only view is incomplete.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a factor that triggers bank runs
questions.stem: A hive bank faces sudden withdrawals after rumors spread.

options.text: Bank runs only occur with zero reserves
High reserves cause bank runs
Loss of depositor confidence can trigger a run
Deposit insurance causes runs

questions.explanation: The formula is one over the reserve ratio. It gives maximum expansion if all excess reserves are lent and redeposited.
questions.hint: Multiplier is one over the ratio.

answer.exemplar: The main liabilities are currency in circulation and bank reserves, both claims on the central bank that back the money supply.

answer.exemplar: New reserves become excess reserves that banks lend, and the loans are redeposited, creating new deposits through repeated rounds until reserves are fully held.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a defense against bank runs
questions.stem: A hive bank seeks to reduce the risk of a depositor run.

options.text: Lower reserves reduce run risk
Deposit insurance and higher reserves reduce run risk
Secrecy about reserves prevents runs
Eliminating deposits prevents runs

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance and adequate reserves reassure depositors and reduce run risk. Lower reserves or secrecy would increase it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the broadest money measure
questions.stem: A logbook lists money measures from narrowest to broadest.

options.text: All measures are equally broad
M3, then M2, then M1
M1, then M2, then M3
Only M1 exists in a hive economy

questions.explanation: Money measures broaden from M1 to M2 to M3 as liquidity falls. M1 is narrowest and M3 is broadest.
questions.hint: Measures broaden from M1 to M3.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the lendable share of deposits
questions.stem: With a reserve ratio of fifteen percent, what share of deposits is lendable?
questions.explanation: Lendable share is one minus the reserve ratio, or zero point eight five. The rest must be held as reserves.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the multiplier from a reserve ratio
questions.stem: What is the simple money multiplier at a reserve ratio of eight percent?
questions.explanation: One divided by zero point zero eight equals twelve point five. A lower ratio raises the multiplier.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why M2 matters for policy
questions.stem: Explain why policymakers track M2 as well as M1 in a hive economy.

answer.exemplar: Policymakers track M2 because it includes near-money assets that can quickly become spendable, giving a broader view of liquidity than M1 alone.

questions.explanation: M2 includes near-money assets that can become spendable, offering a broader liquidity view than M1. Both matter for policy.
